# Pickled Onions

## Ingredients

- 2 red onions, sliced very thin
- 200 ml white vinegar
- 200 ml water
- 1 tablespoon of sugar
- 1 teaspoon of salt
- a jar with a tight lid

## Method

I slice the red onions as thinly as I can with a sharp knife, aiming for half-moon slivers that bend rather than spring. If the slices are too thick they stay crunchy and raw in the middle, so thin is the one thing worth taking time over. I pack the slices loosely into a clean jar and press them down a little, but not so hard that they bruise.

In a small pan I combine equal parts white vinegar and water, so 200 ml of each here, then add a tablespoon of sugar and a teaspoon of salt. I bring the liquid just to the boil and stir until both the sugar and the salt have dissolved completely, which takes less than a minute. I pour the hot liquid straight over the onions in the jar, right to the brim, so the slices are fully covered and the heat starts to do its work on the raw edge.

I let the jar cool on the counter for an hour, then screw the lid on tight and move it to the fridge. The onions are ready to eat after about an hour, when they have turned a bright pink and softened enough to fold, and the flavour deepens over the next day or two. They keep for around a month in the fridge if the liquid stays over them, and I fish them out with a clean fork each time so nothing spoils the brine. A wide-mouthed jar makes them easier to pack and easier to reach into later.

## Notes

Equal parts vinegar and water is the backbone of this recipe, and it is what keeps the onions firm and bright rather than soft and harsh. A stronger vinegar mix pickles them harder and faster but makes them unpleasant to eat on their own, and a weaker one leaves them tasting raw after a week. The sugar is not there to make them sweet; it rounds off the sharpness of the vinegar so the onions taste balanced on the tongue. Pouring the brine hot is what starts the cure instantly and gives you something usable within the hour, which is why these are never sold as a long project. Red onions are the right choice because their colour bleeds into the vinegar and turns the whole jar a vivid pink, and white onions simply do not do that. The onions are very good with tacos, piled on top of slow-cooked pork, and they are just as good with cheese, cutting through something rich like a sharp cheddar or a soft blue. Keep the jar cold, use clean cutlery, and top up the brine with a fresh batch if the onions start to poke above the surface. A jar of these in the fridge is one of the best things to have ready for a quick lunch, and they cost almost nothing to make.
